proposed_edges.relationship: Moral economies of science: certain forms of empiricism, quantification and objectivity “require” a web of affect-saturated values (1995)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (Osiris 10, 1995, pp. 3–4). "certain forms of empiricism, quantification, and objectivity itself are not simply compatible with moral economies; they require moral economies" (p. 3); a moral economy is "a web of affect-saturated values that stand and function in well-defined relationship to one another" (p. 4). n. 2 gathers studies by Hannaway, Porter, Schaffer and Shapin under the rubric. A distinct contribution from the 1992 image article (edge_761); the later book Objectivity (2007, with Galison) is dated in the chronology and read only through a reviewer.

proposed_edges.relationship: Science studies and the history of science diverged during the 1990s: the history of science “became ever more historical and science studies ever less”; science studies stayed “undisciplined”, and historicizing objectivity is not debunking it (2009)
proposed_edges.map_label: Daston: history of science versus science studies, 2009
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read in full (Critical Inquiry 35, 2009). The fields "came to diverge … as the history of science became ever more historical and science studies ever less" (p. 800); science studies read Kuhn "as a manifesto of relativism", historians took from him that "teleology must be repudiated" (p. 802); the history of science "has … become a discipline", while science studies "has remained interdisciplinary—and, even on the testimony of some insiders, undisciplined" (p. 811); its assumptions are "Manichean" (p. 812). In the terms of the Science Wars she answers the relativism charge: "to historicize the category of the fact, objectivity, or proof is not thereby to debunk it" (p. 812); "'If historical, then relative' is a non sequitur" (p. 813), citing Latour's "Why Has Critique Run out of Steam?" (2004). Qualifications: she credits "intensive and fruitful exchanges" in the 1970s and 1980s (p. 800), doubts that disciplinarity is an unmixed good (p. 811 n. 30) and calls for "a new form of interdisciplinarity" (p. 813).

proposed_edges.relationship: Foucault’s historicism and the history of objectivity: Daston credits it with opening “proof, experience, and objectivity” to history (2009), and reviewers compare Objectivity with Foucauldian genealogy while noting its distance from his “epistemes”
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A comparison, not a documented personal borrowing. Her field-level acknowledgement, read (Critical Inquiry, 2009): the counterweight to miniaturizing history of science "has been supplied not by science studies but by a still more thoroughgoing form of historicism, namely, the philosophical history of Michel Foucault" (p. 809); "Topics like proof, experience, and objectivity … suddenly seemed fair game" (p. 810). Readers: Switzer (Foucault Studies 6, 2009, p. 99, read): "though it is unacknowledged, it is by a kind of Foucauldian genealogy that Daston and Galison conduct their study"; Henning (New Formations 64, 2008, read in full by the second research pass): virtues are aimed at through "'techniques of the self' in Foucault's sense, though this is not a straightforwardly Foucaultian argument" (p. 154), and the authors "distance themselves from Foucault's theory of historical rupture" (p. 157). Objectivity itself contrasts its history with "the static tableaux of paradigms and epistemes" (p. 19, as Switzer quotes it); the book is unread here and Galison holds equal credit. Personal transmission can be reconsidered after stronger evidence is read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Two explicitly distinguished uses of “moral economy”: the crowd’s “legitimizing notion” (1971) and the affect-laden values of science (1995)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Daston's own note, read (Osiris 10, 1995, p. 3 n. 1): "my use of the term moral economy diverges significantly from E. P. Thompson's in 'The Moral Economy of the English Crowd in the Eighteenth Century' … My appeal here to 'economies' of affects and values has little to do with Thompson's accounts of corn markets and the tradition of 'setting the price' by persuasion or riot, although it does appeal to a broader sense of 'legitimizing notion.'" A teaching comparison of one term in two fields, not an influence: she says the usage diverges. Thompson's essay is recorded on edge_472.

proposed_edges.relationship: Elias’s civilizing process as a model for the collective self-discipline of scientific observers (1995)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her acknowledgement, read by the second research pass ("The Moral Economy of Science", Osiris 10, 1995, pp. 3–5 and 21–24, in the IAS-hosted scan). n. 7: "I have in mind a gradual shaping of a collective personality akin (and, as will be seen below, sometimes identical) to Norbert Elias's 'civilizing process'"; p. 22: "Norbert Elias argued that all complex coordinations of human activity partake of the 'civilizing process,' that is, the 'permanent self-control' demanded by 'the lengthening of the chains of social action and interdependence,' and science is no exception here." She applies it to the self-effacement of "aperspectival objectivity" (pp. 21–22). Compare elias → roger_chartier (edge_453).

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Weak and mediated (Objectivity p. 19 via Switzer); left out.
Folded into the sts critique, whose evidence records her answer to the relativism charge.

The entry is scoped to the French Bachelard–Canguilhem tradition. The second pass reads her 1995 naming of “historical epistemology” (pp. 23–24) and Sturm (2008); left for Sol as a scope decision on the epistemology entry.

verification.note: Read in part (pp. 3–4) for revision 1.144 in the Max Planck Society PuRe public PDF (item_2276978). p. 3: "I will nonetheless claim that not only does science have what I will call a moral economy (indeed, several); these moral economies are moreover constitutive of those features conventionally (and, to my mind, correctly) deemed most characteristic of science as a way of knowing … certain forms of empiricism, quantification, and objectivity itself are not simply compatible with moral economies; they require moral economies." p. 3 n. 1: "my use of the term moral economy diverges significantly from E. P. Thompson's in 'The Moral Economy of the English Crowd in the Eighteenth Century' … My appeal here to 'economies' of affects and values has little to do with Thompson's accounts of corn markets … although it does appeal to a broader sense of 'legitimizing notion.'" n. 2 gathers Hannaway, Porter, Schaffer and Shapin. p. 4: "a web of affect-saturated values that stand and function in well-defined relationship to one another"; "As Gaston Bachelard decades ago remarked, to imbue objects or actions with emotion is almost always thereby to valorize them". pp. 5–24 unread. The second research pass (evidence-daston.pass2.md §1) read pp. 3–5 and 21–24 in another scan (www.ias.edu/sites/default/files/sss/pdfs/Moral-Daston.pdf): p. 5, "To extend Ludwik Fleck's terminology, what is meant here is a Gefühls- as well as a Denkkollektiv", n. 7 and p. 22 on Elias's "civilizing process", pp. 21–22 on mechanical and "aperspectival objectivity", and pp. 23–24: moral economies "are part of what one might call historical epistemology—a history of the categories of facticity, evidence, objectivity, and so forth". That pass cites the article as pp. 2–24; the article's first page prints "OSIRIS 1995, 10: 3-24" and p. 2 is the frontispiece, so 3–24 is kept.

verification.note: Read in part (pp. 96–99) for revision 1.144 (open PDF). Quotes Objectivity: "[T]his history is one of innovation and proliferation rather than monarchic succession … new stars winking into existence, not replacing old ones but changing the geography of the heavens" (p. 18, at Switzer p. 96); "In contrast to the static tableaux of paradigms and epistemes, this is a history of dynamic fields" (p. 19, at p. 97); "All history can do is to demonstrate the possibility of alternatives" (p. 376, at p. 98). Switzer: "Implicitly, it is Kuhnian history that Lorraine Daston and Peter Galison have in mind" (p. 96); history is "exempted from the questions that confront a science when its epistemology is historicized" (p. 98); "though it is unacknowledged, it is by a kind of Foucauldian genealogy that Daston and Galison conduct their study" (p. 99). Objectivity itself is unread.
